text: Course 11's lesson on testing DR made the core case: a tabletop exercise narrates a runbook, a real drill executes it, and only the real drill proves anything about RTO or RPO. At enterprise scale, that principle doesn't change — but 'just run it for real' gets a lot harder when running it for real means failing over one piece of a web of dozens of interdependent services instead of one application.

You can't tabletop-walk sixty services, and you genuinely can't fail all sixty over at once on live traffic either — that's not a drill, that's an outage you scheduled yourself. Real enterprise DR testing at this scale is scoped: pick one service or one dependency chain, using the graph from Lesson 14 to know exactly what else is in that chain's blast radius, and test that slice on real production traffic, not a staging copy that can't reproduce real data volume, warmed caches, or how an actual third-party integration behaves under load.

The mechanics look like a canary release applied to failover: shift a small percentage of real traffic — two percent, say — to the DR region, and watch error rate and latency for several minutes before deciding anything. If it holds, ramp further: ten percent, fifty, then a full cutover. If it doesn't, an automatic, pre-tested rollback reverts the traffic shift immediately. The rollback path has to be drilled before the test, not improvised during it — a DR test with no tested way back is just an outage with extra steps.

Scoping the test uses the same dependency graph that scopes a real failure. If checkout's blast radius is checkout, pricing-service, and inventory-service, that's the boundary of this drill — reporting and a notifications batch job that don't sit in checkout's live-traffic path get excluded and tested on their own schedule, not pulled into a test that was never about them.

That's the whole chapter's arc: revisit active-active and active-passive at real enterprise complexity, map the dependencies so blast radius means something specific, automate the failover so it doesn't depend on who's awake at three a.m., and test all of it on live production traffic in safely scoped slices with a rollback ready before you ever need it. Chapter 5 turns to a related discipline — forecasting capacity and load-testing before a traffic spike arrives, instead of reacting to one.
